implicate

/IM-plih-kayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Implicate means to show or suggest, through evidence, that someone was involved in a crime or wrongdoing.

Grainy security footage seemed to implicate the night-shift supervisor in the warehouse break-in, though he insisted he had only been checking a tripped alarm.

Worked Example

The forensic accountant's report appeared to implicate the nonprofit's treasurer in the disappearance of nearly forty thousand dollars in donations.

The report's financial evidence connects the treasurer to the missing money — it suggests her involvement without formally charging her with anything, which is exactly what implicate means.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

compromise: To compromise someone is to damage their standing or leave them exposed to suspicion — leaked emails can compromise an official without showing any wrongdoing at all. To implicate someone, the evidence must point to their actual involvement in the deed itself, not merely dent their reputation.

entangle: To entangle someone is to catch them in something messy and hard to escape — paperwork, a lawsuit, a feud — with no claim about guilt at all. To implicate them is sharper: evidence suggests they took part in the wrongdoing itself.

embroil: To embroil someone is to drag them into a conflict or scandal, where the emphasis is the turmoil around them. To implicate them is quieter and more pointed: a document or a fingerprint suggests their own involvement in the wrong, whether or not any public storm follows.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

exonerate: to officially clear someone of blame

exculpate: to show that someone is not guilty

Where it sits · how strongly evidence points to guilt — associate → implicate → incriminate

associate vs. implicate: To associate someone with a scandal merely links their name to it loosely; to implicate them means real evidence points to their actual involvement.

incriminate vs. implicate: To implicate someone suggests involvement in wrongdoing; to incriminate them means the evidence points squarely at their guilt.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: in, into (form of 'in-' before p)

Root — plic

Root — plic: to fold (Latin plicare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming suffix: to make or do

Put it together

Put it together: Implicate literally means 'to fold in' — evidence folds a person into a crime, wrapping them up inside its story.

Use the root in a new word: replicate

Use the root in a new word: replicate: The lab team tried to replicate the study's results — literally to 'fold' the experiment 'again' — repeating each step to produce an exact copy of the outcome.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / legal & journalistic

Implicate appears constantly in reporting on investigations: documents, footage, or testimony implicates a person — it suggests their involvement. Keep it distinct from indict (also taught in this unit), which is the formal legal act of charging someone with a crime: evidence can implicate a person for years without them ever being indicted.
